title: Mine is Giridhar Gopal
hookLine: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else
carry: belonging to God loosens the world's shame
tomorrow: how can a woman who left a palace call herself rich?

cards: Some songs argue. Some plead. This one simply states a fact, the way you'd give someone your address.
Mere to Giridhar Gopal, doosro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. It's one of the songs sung in Mira's voice, short enough to carry in your pocket.
And it closes a week of singers who each found a way to belong.

teach.b: Mine is Giridhar Gopal, the mountain-lifter, the cowherd, and no one else. The one who wears the peacock-feather crown, he is my husband. That word, husband, is the scandal and the point.

Bhakti poets often picture the soul as a bride and God as the beloved; Mira sings it as her life. Tradition says she was married to a prince. In the song, she says plainly that she belongs to someone else.
Then she counts the cost. Father, mother, brothers, relatives: she has let them go.
Sitting among the holy ones, she says, I've lost lok laj, the world's sense of shame. What can anyone do to me now? Then an image that's hard to forget.

teach.h: TEARS WATERED THE VINE OF LOVE.
teach.b: With my tears, again and again, I watered the vine of love. Now it has spread, and it bears its fruit of joy. Notice the order.
Not: I belong to no one, so I'm free. The reverse: I belong so completely to one that the world's opinion has lost its grip. That's a logic of bhakti, folded into one song.
Now the week. Bhakti teachers name several moods of love for God. Tulsidas gave Hanuman's song, a servant's love.
Surdas stood in Yashoda's yard with a parent's love, and gave the gopis their answer: our one mind went with Shyam. And Mira, a bride's love: mine is Giridhar.
Three singers, one shape. Each belongs to someone, and the belonging sets the song free.

how: Mere to Giridhar Gopal is sung as a bhajan in homes, temples and concerts, often in a simple call-and-response that lets anyone join the refrain.

o: songs the Rana's court wrote to praise its queen
songs in which Mira calls Krishna her husband
lullabies Yashoda sang to the baby Krishna

games.q: line by line — tap the pairs.
p: the one she calls her husband

s: in the song, Mira says she belongs to no one
mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else.
she sings that her tears watered a vine of love
again and again, until it spread and bore its fruit of joy.
in the song, she keeps her family's approval
she says she let family go and lost the world's sense of shame.

games.q: you're Mira. your husband's family says the temple, the dancing and the holy men are shaming the house. stop, they say. what do you do?
o: stop, and keep your devotion private.
keep going: I've lost the world's shame; mine is Giridhar.
put away Krishna's image and return to court life.
games.why: in her songs she keeps going: what can anyone do to me now? the belonging comes first, and the freedom follows from it.

practice: Let the breath come and go slowly, like water poured on a young vine, and ask one plain question: whose am I? Not what do I do, but whose: a person, a community, God, a promise you keep.
Let the answer come in your own words or none, notice whether some opinion out there has a little less grip on you, and if you pray, rest in the one you belong to.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai's songs. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else: belonging so complete that the world's shame lost its hold.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: the cowherd, a name of Krishna, as in mere to Giridhar Gopal.

carryVoice: Your line: belonging to God loosens the world's shame. Belonging came first, and the freedom followed. Tomorrow: how can a woman who left a palace call herself rich?
